lesson.title: Policing the Backyard: Roosevelt Rewrites the Monroe Doctrine
lesson.summary: In 1904 Theodore Roosevelt reinterpreted the Monroe Doctrine to claim the United States had the right to intervene in Latin American nations to head off European intervention, a policy that defined U.S. dominance in the Western Hemisphere for decades.
lesson.body:
The Monroe Doctrine, announced by President James Monroe in 1823, had always been mostly defensive. It warned European powers not to establish new colonies or reassert control in the Americas, but it did not claim any right for the United States to interfere in how Latin American nations ran their own affairs. By the early 1900s, though, Theodore Roosevelt saw a new problem. Several Latin American governments, including the Dominican Republic, owed large debts to European banks, and Roosevelt worried that Germany, Britain, or other powers might use unpaid debts as an excuse to send warships and seize territory or customs houses, much as a coalition of European powers had briefly blockaded Venezuela in 1902 and 1903 to collect debts.

Roosevelt's solution, announced in his annual message to Congress in December 1904, became known as the Roosevelt Corollary. He argued that if Latin American nations kept their affairs in order, the United States would not interfere, but if a nation engaged in what he called chronic wrongdoing or instability that invited European intervention, the United States itself would exercise an international police power in the Western Hemisphere. In practice, this meant the United States would step in first, rather than let European creditors do so. The following year, U.S. officials took over the collection of customs revenue in the Dominican Republic to ensure its debts were paid, and similar interventions followed in Cuba, Nicaragua, Haiti, and elsewhere in the years afterward.

The Roosevelt Corollary transformed the Monroe Doctrine from a promise to keep Europe out into a justification for American intervention across Latin America and the Caribbean. It reflected Roosevelt's broader philosophy of foreign policy, often summarized by his own saying about speaking softly while carrying a big stick, meaning the United States should back its diplomacy with credible military strength and a willingness to use it. This assertive approach set a pattern that his successors would continue, sometimes with different tools. The next chapter shows how President William Howard Taft attempted a variation on this same goal, using American dollars rather than American gunboats, though with results that were not always so different in practice.
